Case Study 4: Andean Shade-Grown Arabica Coffee · Regulation (EU) 2023/1115
Shade-Grown Arabica Coffee Rejuvenation versus Protected Montane Cloud-Forest Encroachment under the EU Deforestation Regulation: Multi-Sensor Verification and Deceptive Claim Interception in Huila, Colombia
Oxeous Spatial Compliance Research Group1,*, Prepared for Department of Geoinformatics — Z_GIS2
1Oxeous Earth Observation & Automated Statutory Compliance Systems (DDS Dossier Ref: C716-CO-2026-HUILA-COFFEE); 2Paris Lodron University of Salzburg (PLUS), Schillerstraße 30, 5020 Salzburg, Austria. *Statutory Cutoff: 31 December 2020.

Abstract: Colombia is the world’s leading supplier of washed specialty Arabica coffee (Coffea arabica, CN 0901 11 00) to the European Union, with Huila Department producing over 18% of the national harvest across high-altitude Andean micro-lots (fincas, 1,450–1,950 m a.s.l.). Under Articles 2(5), 3(a), 3(b), and 10(2)(f) of the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR, Regulation (EU) 2023/1115), Andean shade-grown coffee cooperatives confront three critical verification failures in conventional two-dimensional (2D) optical monitoring and text-based auditing. First, traditional Inga edulis (guamo) shade-coffee agroforestry maintains 35–50% canopy cover (h > 8 m); when farmers perform mandatory 5-year agronomical coffee stumping (zoca / recepa) and shade-tree crown thinning under Federación Nacional de Cafeteros (FNC / Cenicafé) protocols, standard 2D forest-loss detectors (Hansen GFC v1.13) misclassify 78% of lawful rejuvenation as illegal deforestation. Second, text-based compliance workflows trust self-reported supplier declarations claiming that post-2020 mountain forest clearings occurred “prior to 2020” (text-trust greenwashing). Third, unsegregated dry-mill (trilladora) batching allows parchment coffee from plots encroaching upon Colombia’s Protected Sub-Andean Montane Cloud-Forest Corridors (Decree 2372/2010, Corredor Biológico Guácharos–Puracé) or inflated “paper coffee” volumes to contaminate entire export lots. This study presents an empirical multi-sensor adjudication of a four-finca cooperative export batch (CO-HUILA-CAFE-2026, 101.00 ha total across Fincas F-01 to F-04) in the Acevedo–Pitalito corridor, Huila, Colombia (1.820°N, 75.892°W). By fusing Sentinel-2 10 m L2A optical time series, Sentinel-1 C-band SAR backscatter (Δγ0), the Nature Trace Natural Forests 2020 baseline, native WDPA/SINAP protected-area vectors, and the Forest Data Partnership (FDP) 10 m deep-learning coffee probability model (coffee/model_2026a) within Oxeous’s PWRI-3D framework, we prove that the 6.80 ha 2022 canopy disturbance in Finca F-03 (21.80 ha) is lawful Article 2(5) zoca rejuvenation on a pre-2020 coffee farm (pcoffee = 93.4%, natural forest 1.4%). Simultaneously, Oxeous refutes a deceptive supplier declaration on Finca F-04 (26.20 ha) claiming “2018 pre-cutoff clearing,” proving via multi-temporal NDVI (0.85 → 0.31) and SAR (Δγ0 = −4.4 dB) that 9.40 ha of primary montane cloud forest (pcoffee = 2.9%, natural forest 97.4%) were cleared in Q3 2022 inside the Guácharos–Puracé protected buffer corridor. Excising F-04 at the dry-mill intake gate and enforcing the FNC/Cenicafé biological yield ceiling (Yc = 2.40 t ha−1 yr−1) blocks 86.0 t of laundered coffee while certifying the remaining 74.80 ha compliant cooperative supply shed (F-01–F-03; 138,400 kg Excelso Green Arabica, €665,000 value) for EU TRACES NT customs clearance.

Keywords: EU Deforestation Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1115); Shade-Grown Arabica Coffee (Coffea arabica); Article 2(5) Zoca Rotational Stumping; Deceptive Supplier Claim Interception; Forest Data Partnership 10 m Coffee Model (coffee/model_2026a); Huila, Colombia.
1. Introduction: The Andean Shade-Coffee Paradox

Washed Arabica coffee (Coffea arabica, CN 0901 11 00) cultivated across the steep slopes of the Colombian Andes represents one of the most structurally complex agro-ecosystems governed by EUDR Article 9(1)(d). In southern Huila Department (Acevedo, Pitalito, and San Agustín municipalities), coffee is predominantly grown by smallholder cooperative members under nitrogen-fixing leguminous shade trees (Inga edulis, Erythrina poeppigiana, and Cordia alliodora). To sustain cherry productivity and control coffee leaf rust (Hemileia vastatrix), FNC and Cenicafé technical guidelines mandate rotational stumping (zoca or recepa) of coffee bushes to a 30 cm stem every 5 to 6 years, accompanied by selective pollarding of overhead Inga shade crowns to regulate solar radiation during vegetative resprouting.

From medium-resolution optical satellites, an established Inga-shaded coffee parcel exhibits closed-canopy near-infrared reflectance (NDVI = 0.78–0.81) that closely mimics native sub-Andean forest. When a farmer executes a 5–7 ha zoca rejuvenation cycle and shade pruning after December 31, 2020, global tree-cover loss algorithms (Hansen GFC v1.13 lossyear > 20) register an abrupt canopy drop and flag the parcel as illegal deforestation. Across Andean shade-coffee cooperatives, conventional 2D optical GIS screening generates a 78.0% false-rejection rate on zoca plots, threatening thousands of biodiversity-friendly shade-coffee smallholders with exclusion from European markets.

Conversely, high-altitude specialty coffee commands substantial price premiums (85+ SCA cupping scores), incentivizing rapid expansion into adjacent upper-watershed cloud forests (Bosque Subandino y Altoandino, 1,800–2,200 m a.s.l.) bordering Colombia’s National Natural Parks system

(SINAP / WDPA, Decree 2372/2010). To evade EUDR screening, non-compliant suppliers frequently submit deceptive textual declarations asserting that newly bulldozed cloud-forest plots were “cleared in 2018–2019 prior to the EUDR cutoff.” When compliance platforms rely on text-only Large Language Models (LLMs) to parse supplier questionnaires without independent pixel-level satellite verification, they trust these deceptive claims, producing catastrophic false passes.

2. Study Area & Cooperative Cadastre (Huila, Colombia)

We evaluate a four-finca cooperative export consignment, Cooperativa Cafetera del Macizo Huilense (Batch CO-HUILA-CAFE-2026), situated in the Acevedo–Pitalito Andean corridor of southern Huila, Colombia (geographic centroid 1.820°N, 75.892°W; WGS84 EPSG:4326). The declared cooperative supply shed spans 101.00 ha divided into four road-bounded mountain micro-lots:

Finca F-01 (CO-HUI-01, Vereda La Esmeralda Alta, 28.40 ha) and Finca F-02 (CO-HUI-02, Vereda El Mirador Central, 24.60 ha) comprise established pre-2012 Castillo and Caturra shade-grown Arabica plots bounded by rural mountain ridge roads (vías veredales). Finca F-03 (CO-HUI-03, Vereda San Isidro, 21.80 ha) is an established pre-2010 shade-grown coffee plot where 6.80 ha underwent rotational zoca stumping and Inga shade-tree crown thinning in Q1 2022. East of the main ridge road, Finca F-04 (CO-HUI-04, Cerro Guácharos Fringe, 26.20 ha) extends across the statutory Guácharos–Puracé Protected Montane Biological Corridor boundary, where 9.40 ha of primary sub-Andean cloud forest were cleared in Q3 2022—accompanied by a deceptive supplier claim (“cleared in 2018”) and an inflated cooperative volume declaration of 224,400 kg green coffee.

3. Methodology: PWRI-3D Shade-Coffee & Yield Gate

To disentangle lawful 5-year zoca coffee stumping and Inga shade pruning (EUDR Article 2(5)) from illegal sub-Andean cloud-forest conversion and deceptive supplier declarations (Articles 3(a) and 3(b)), Oxeous evaluates every 10 m pixel (x, y) using Rule 1: PWRI-3D Agroforestry vs. Montane Forest Discrimination. Post-2020 canopy disturbance pixels (Losspost-2020 from Hansen GFC v1.13 and Sentinel-2 L2A) are intersected against the dual 2020 baseline of the Nature Trace / WRI 10 m Natural Forests 2020 probability layer (pnat,2020) and the Forest Data Partnership 10 m deep-learning coffee probability model (pcoffee,2020 from coffee/model_2026a):

V3(a) = MMU≥0.5ha(Losspost-2020 ∩ {pnat ≥ 0.50}) ∖ {pcoffee ≥ 0.90 ∧ ΔNDVI > +0.18}
(1)

A canopy disturbance cluster qualifies as exempt Article 2(5) zoca rejuvenation if and only if: (i) the 2020 FDP 10 m model confirms pre-cutoff coffee occupancy (pcoffee ≥ 0.90) and negligible natural forest probability (pnat < 0.05); (ii) Sentinel-1 C-band SAR confirms intact terraced root structure and absence of timber slash-and-burn clearing (Δγ0 > −1.8 dB); and (iii) Sentinel-2 phenology tracks rapid vegetative resprouting (ΔNDVI > +0.18 within 18–24 months). Second, at the cooperative dry-mill level, any micro-lot Fk exhibiting V3(a)(Fk) > 0 or encroaching upon a SINAP/WDPA Protected Montane Biological Corridor (ZWDPA, Decree 2372/2010) is excised prior to parchment intake:

P′coop = ∪ { Fk ∣ V3(a)(Fk) = 0 ∧ A(Fk ∩ ZWDPA) = 0 } = F01 ∪ F02 ∪ F03
(2)

Third, to prevent coffee harvested from excised F-04 or external non-compliant farms from being laundered through the certified polygon P′coop (74.80 ha), Agent A6 enforces the FNC/Cenicafé 99th-percentile biological Arabica yield ceiling (Yc = 2.40 t green coffee ha−1 yr−1):

Yimplied = Mgreen / AWGS84(P′coop) = 138.4 t / 74.80 ha = 1.85 t ha−1 ≤ Yc
(3)
4. Empirical Results & Deceptive Claim Proof

As demonstrated in Figure 1 and Table 1, Oxeous resolves all three compliance failure modes simultaneously. In Fincas F-01 (28.40 ha) and F-02 (24.60 ha), Inga-shaded Arabica canopies remained stable from 2019 through 2025 (NDVI 0.79–0.80; FDP coffee probability 96.2% and 94.8%). In Finca F-03 (21.80 ha), 6.80 ha of 6-year-old Castillo coffee rows underwent rotational zoca stumping and shade pollarding in Q1 2022, causing a temporary NDVI dip from 0.78 to 0.56 (Figure 2a). While 2D Hansen GFC alerts flagged F-03 as 6.80 ha of deforestation, the clipped FDP 10 m probability surface (Figure 1b) proves that 93.4% of F-03 was established coffee prior to 2020 (Nature Trace natural forest 1.4%). Vigorous orthotropic stem resprouting restored NDVI to 0.78 by 2025-Q1, certifying F-03 under EUDR Article 2(5).

Conversely, on Finca F-04 (26.20 ha), the supplier declared: “Heritage family coffee plot cleared in 2018; zero post-2020 loss.” While a text-only LLM baseline trusted this pre-2020 date and issued a critical False PASS, Oxeous’s multi-sensor time series refutes the claim: F-04 exhibited an undisturbed montane cloud-forest canopy (NDVI 0.85–0.86; 97.4% Nature Trace natural forest; only 2.9% FDP coffee probability) continuously from 2019 through Q1 2022, before suffering an abrupt 9.40 ha slash-and-burn collapse in August 2022 (NDVI 0.85 → 0.31; Sentinel-1 SAR Δγ0 = −4.4 dB) inside the Guácharos–Puracé protected corridor (Figure 2a). Moreover, when the cooperative attempted to declare 224.4 t of green coffee across the surviving 74.80 ha polygon P′coop (3.00 t ha−1 > 2.40 t ha−1 ceiling; Figure 2b), Agent A6 blocked the 86.0 t laundered excess and certified the true 138,400 kg Excelso export lot (1.85 t ha−1).

5. Discussion & Policy Conclusions

This study demonstrates that automated EUDR verification in Andean specialty coffee cannot rely on text-based LLM questionnaires or single-layer tree-loss alerts. By fusing the 10 m Forest Data Partnership coffee probability baseline (coffee/model_2026a) with multi-temporal Sentinel-2/SAR trajectories, native WDPA/SINAP protected-corridor vectors, and the FNC/Cenicafé biological yield cap, Oxeous simultaneously eliminates the 78.0% zoca false-rejection crisis on Finca F-03, intercepts the deceptive “2018 clearing” declaration on Finca F-04, blocks 86,000 kg of laundered coffee, and certifies 138,400 kg of compliant shade-grown Excelso Arabica (€665,000 export value).
